newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea bank arrest underlines deregulation need.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea bank arrest underlines deregulation need.

text.p: The arrest of the head of a leading South Korean bank over the weekend underlined the need for a drastic restructuring of the country's ailing banking industry, analysts said on Monday.
But whether the government is ready to make deep enough changes is not entirely certain.

On Saturday, state prosecutors arrested SEOULBANK president Sohn Hong-gyun on charges of taking $121,000 in kickbacks in return for loans. SEOULBANK is the nation's sixth biggest bank in terms of deposits.
"This (arrest) could set up momentum for structural changes in the banking industry," said Shinyoung Securities' market analyst Steven Lee.

Kim Byong-suk, a banking analyst at Hannuri-Salomon Securities, said: "There are a lot of illegal loan extensions going on. Banks will want to clean up their acts after this, and could cut credit lines to weak companies. This will be positive in the long-term."

Seoul plans to allow mergers and acquisitions between banks from next year to sharpen competitiveness ahead of opening the doors to foreign banks in 1998. However, the takeovers would take place under the watchful eyes of the government and would not be purely market-driven, some analysts said.

"The government is still quite powerful in banking management, and it wants to continue that control rather than introduce more efficient systems," said a banking analyst at a foreign securities house who asked not to be identified.
"The scandal investigation is seen publicly as a step toward a more democratic (management), but banking management will continue to stay under government control," he added.

Analysts said the South Korean banking industry is plagued by a variety of ills, including heavily government-influenced policies, lack of proper credit analyses, and poorly-performing stock market investments.
The slow-down in the economy has further pressured loan quality and the bottom line as bankruptcies among small- and medium-sized firms rise.
At the end of last year 25 local commercial banks had a combined total of 2.29 trillion won in bad loans, up 19 percent from a year earlier, a Hyundai Securities report said.
Banks are also hampered by a history of being a government tool, providing cheap loans for development projects during South Korea's post-war reconstruction.

"Banks have a lot of problems in Korea because they are still considered by the society as public entities, not private ones, which should sacrifice for the public good," said a local broker. "If they earn too much profit, they are criticised by the press and the public."

Sohn is the latest prominent banker to be involved in a corruption scandal. Fourteen other bank heads, including two previous SEOULBANK heads, have been arrested or sacked for involvement in irregularities since President Kim Young-sam took office in 1993.
But some analysts believe this scandal will be a watershed, as time is running out for corrupt management.

"The current situation is different from the past. The government will designate banks with bad records as takeover targets," said Hannuri's Kim. "If they are merged, most top management will be fired, and they don't want that to happen."
